title: Oscillation and Transient Error Runbook + Status Templates
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview:
This runbook covers detection, immediate mitigation, and post-incident steps for service oscillation and transient error patterns in the LLM inference stack. 'Oscillation' refers to short-timescale cycles of high latency -> autoscale -> overload -> scale-down -> repeat caused by interaction between request batching, KV cache pressure, model cold-starts, and upstream rate variations. The playbook also includes status page and customer communication templates tailored to oscillation scenarios.

Scope and audience:
- Applies to: Redwood inference frontend, request-router, batcher, runtime GPU pools and autoscaler controllers.
- Intended readers: on-call engineers (SRE/serving), product owners for affected routes, support/CS for customer comms.

Definitions:
- Oscillation: repeating cycles of degraded request latency and recovery within a short window (minutes).
- Transient error: non-deterministic 5xx/timeout errors that resolve with retry or route failover.
- Batch storm: sudden influx of concurrent requests that leads to oversized batches and queueing.

SLOs / alert thresholds (examples):
- 99th percentile latency (inference) > 800ms for 2 consecutive 1m windows -> alert P2.
- Error rate (5xx) > 1% and increasing vs baseline for 5m -> alert P1.
- Autoscaler thrash (>= 3 scale events for same nodepool within 10m) -> alert P2.
- Queue depth > 95th percentile of historic distribution and growing -> alert P1.

Primary signals to examine (dashboards):
- per-route token throughput and qps
- queue depth and average batch size
- per-GPU active KV cache memory usage and eviction rate
- model cold-start time and kernel initialization logs
- autoscaler events and pod lifecycle events
- request latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99)
- 5xx/timeout error traces and correlated client IDs

Immediate triage (first 10m) - numbered steps:
1. Acknowledge alert and open incident bridge (use standard bridge template).
2. Determine scope: which routes/models and which regions are affected. Check per-route tag + region filters.
3. Inspect queue length and batch size metrics: identify if average batch size jumped > 2x baseline.
4. Check autoscaler events (kubectl get events, or autoscaler dashboard). Note if frequent scale-ups and scale-downs are present.
5. Look for KV cache pressure: check eviction_rate and mem_worst_peak for model shards. High eviction suggests cache churn.
6. If error rate high, capture representative request IDs and trace to identify common failure point (e.g., runtime exception vs network).
7. If customer-impacting (>= 10% of requests or paying-customer errors), notify Customer Success immediately and prepare a status update.

Immediate mitigations (minutes) - choose concurrently as safe:
- Apply global outlier protection: temporarily enable per-route concurrency cap to reduce oversized batches. CLI example:
  - curl -X POST https://control-plane/api/routes/<route>/overrides -d '{"max_concurrency": 8, "max_batch": 16}'
- Pin traffic away from noisy region/model variant: update routing policy to fallback variant or another region.
- Pause autoscaler scale-in window for impacted nodepools (prevent thrash): kubectl annotate nodepool/<np> autoscaler.k8s.io/scale-down-disabled=true
- Reduce prefetching/shift batching timeout to lower batch sizes: set batcher.timeout_ms=25 (example).
- If KV cache is thrashing, increase KV cache capacity for short window or reduce model shard packing to reduce working set.

Mitigation decision matrix (quick reference):
- If latency increased but errors are low: throttle concurrency and reduce batch timeout.
- If errors (5xx/timeouts) spike and autoscaler thrash: disable scale-in and route traffic to a fallback model variant.
- If single customer is spiking: apply rate limit to that API key and engage CS for customer-side mitigation.

Commands and snippets (examples):
- Inspect pods and events:
  kubectl -n redwood get pods -l app=runtime --sort-by=.status.startTime
  kubectl -n redwood describe hpa runtime-hpa
- View batcher metrics (promql):
  sum(rate(batcher_requests_total[1m])) by (route)
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(batcher_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
- Check KV cache evictions (redis or internal metrics):
  redis-cli INFO memory | grep used_memory_human

Escalation and ownership matrix:
- On-call responder: owns initial triage and mitigation (first 30m).
- Runtime team lead: owner for kernel/cold-start and model runtime issues.
- Autoscaler owner: resolves scale thrash and node pool adjustments.
- CS lead: coordinates customer comms when paying customers impacted.
- Security: notify if evidence of abuse or malicious traffic pattern.

Status page templates (short / long):
- Short (initial, low-certainty):
  "Investigating: We are seeing elevated latency and transient errors for inference requests in US-West. Our engineers are investigating the root cause and applying mitigations. We will update in 30 minutes. Impact: some requests may time out or be delayed."
- Follow-up (mitigation in place):
  "Mitigating: We have applied temporary traffic limiting and routing changes to reduce request backpressure. Error rate has decreased by X% and p99 latency is improving, but some customers may still see reduced throughput. We will continue to monitor and post a status update in 15-30 minutes."
- Resolved (post-recovery):
  "Resolved: We identified a traffic pattern that caused repeated autoscaler scale/unstable batches and have applied a permanent fix to rate limiting and batch configuration. All services are operating within expected SLOs. A follow-up postmortem will be posted in 48 hours."

Customer communication templates (CS / support):
- Short notice to affected customers (template):
  Subject: Service disruption affecting inference latency

  Hi <CustomerName>,

  We are investigating increased latency and intermittent errors affecting inference requests for <Project/Route>. Our engineers have applied mitigation steps to reduce impact while we finish root cause analysis. You may see delayed or retried requests; we recommend temporary client-side retries with exponential backoff (initial 200ms, max 2s) until we confirm full recovery.

  We'll send an update within 30 minutes and follow with a summary once we complete the postmortem.

  Sorry for the disruption — the Redwood SRE team

- Detailed follow-up (post-incident):
  Subject: Incident summary — inference oscillation on <date>

  Hi <CustomerName>,

  Summary: On <date/time> we observed an oscillation pattern impacting <routes>. Impact: up to X% increased latency and Y% request failures for approximately Z minutes. Root cause: interaction of a sudden request pattern with batcher timeout settings and autoscaler scale-in aggressiveness causing repeated oversized batches and KV cache evictions.

  Mitigation: temporarily limited per-key concurrency, adjusted batch timeout from 100ms -> 30ms, and paused scale-in for the affected nodepool. Longer-term fix: revert autoscaler scale-in policy changes and deploy batcher heuristic that caps batch growth on heavy variance.

  Action items and timeline: [list with owners and ETA]

  If you need a dedicated call for impact analysis, reply and we'll schedule.

  Regards,
  Customer Success & SRE

On-call rotation and handoff checklist (concise):
- Before shift: confirm primary/secondary listed in rota and that buildkite/ops notifications route to personal channels.
- At shift start: run quick health checks: p99 latency, error rate, queue depth for top 10 routes.
- Handoff notes (always):
  - Current active incidents (link + short status)
  - Any temporary mitigations or annotations on routes
  - Top risks to watch for the next 4 hours (e.g., scheduled deploys, large customer jobs)
- At shift end: update incident if present, and confirm next owner acknowledged.

Game day scenario: Batch Storm & Oscillation (30–60m exercise)
- Goal: Practice rapid triage and mitigation for oscillation caused by synthetic traffic spike.
- Setup: spin up canary route with traffic generator (1k rps burst) targeted at a single model variant, and instrument dashboards to show batch size, p99, and autoscaler events.
- Steps:
  1. Start burst; wait for alerts to fire.
  2. On-call practices runbook steps: throttle, adjust batch timeout, pin fallback variant, pause scale-in.
  3. Observe recovery and reverse mitigations.
- Metrics to evaluate: time to acknowledge, time-to-first-mitigation, time to p99 < 800ms, correctness of customer comms.

Postmortem checklist (post-incident actions):
- Capture timeline (UTC) with evidence and owner for each event.
- Attach dashboard snapshots and representative traces.
- List root cause analysis and why mitigations worked/didn't.
- Action items with owner and ETA (categorize: immediate, short-term, long-term).
- Decide if change requires scheduled maintenance window or hotfix.
- Share with stakeholders within 48 hours and schedule retrospective with involved teams.

Notes and long-term mitigations (examples):
- Implement adaptive batching heuristic that decays batch growth rate when variance in arrival is high.
- Make autoscaler scale-in more conservative for nodepools serving critical customers.
- Add a per-key burst allowance and automated soft-limit escalation to avoid noisy-tenant impact.
- Invest in richer KV cache telemetry (per-shard working set) and alarm on eviction-induced latency increases.

References and links:
- Runtime architecture: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture
- Incident comms templates: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-comm-and-postmortem-framework-2026

Appendix: sample incident bridge script (quick run)
1) Open bridge call: /ops/bridge new --title "Oscillation - <route> - <region>" --severity P1
2) Pin dashboards: runtime/p99, batcher/queue, autoscaler/events
3) Post first status to status page using control-plane CLI:
  redwood status post --component inference --message "Investigating elevated latency and transient errors in US-West. Engineers are on it." --impact partial
